findings.location: build/web/claude/liturgy/roman-rite/1962/propers/temporal/57-seventeenth-after-pentecost.md, whole document (the PDF's Contents page, p. 1, has no counterpart)
findings.problem: The study's PDF carries a full Contents page listing all ten sections and their subsections with page numbers; main.tex requests it with \tableofcontents. The conversion drops it: tools/web-edition line 983 removes \tableofcontents outright and whitelists it as a layout macro, so the web edition is one page of roughly 19,700 words with no navigation of any kind. Nothing informational is lost -- every heading the Contents lists is present, in order, with a working anchor, and page numbers mean nothing after reflow -- so this is not a content omission and the converter's behaviour is deliberate rather than accidental. It is nonetheless an asymmetry that falls on exactly the reader the web edition exists for, the one who cannot use the print-shaped PDF, and it bites harder here than on any earlier leaf: this is the first proper leaf whose main.tex asks for a table of contents at all, and the study is the longest in the corpus. The site's renderer already loads Python Markdown's toc extension (scripts/_markdown_render.py), so a [TOC] marker would render a live contents list; no tracked web edition currently uses one.
findings.required_result: Either the canonical web edition offers in-page navigation equivalent to the PDF's Contents -- for example the converter emitting a [TOC] marker for a leaf whose entrypoint requests \tableofcontents, which the site's already-enabled toc extension would render as a linked heading list -- or the decision to drop print navigation for long studies is recorded where a reviewer meets it, beside the \multicolumn and \< handlings in the Fidelity section of guidance/web-editions.md, so that the next review meets the decision instead of the bare gap.

findings.location: build/web/claude/liturgy/roman-rite/1962/propers/temporal/57-seventeenth-after-pentecost.md lines 289-299, 361-371 and 425-435 (the three 'The four senses of this reading' blocks)
findings.problem:
In the source the four senses are a description list (fourSenses in format.tex, \item[Literal.] and the rest), so the PDF sets each sense name as a bold term with its distillation hanging beside it. The conversion emits each as a plain paragraph whose first line is the bare label followed by a hard line break: 'Literal. \n In the Temple, Jesus answers...', rendering as

Literal.
In the Temple...

with no emphasis and no list structure. The four senses remain present, correctly named, in order and separated, so nothing is lost or confusable, but the one structural feature the three-documents contract makes mandatory for every interpretation is the one place in the document where the source's own typographic distinction between a label and its body is dropped rather than adapted, and a sense name in running weight at the head of a paragraph is easy to read straight through.
findings.required_result: The four sense labels carry, in the rendered page, a weight or structure that marks them as labels rather than as the first word of the paragraph -- a definition list, or bold terms -- so that the four senses of each reading are as scannable on the web as they are in the PDF.

findings.location: build/web/claude/liturgy/roman-rite/1962/propers/temporal/57-seventeenth-after-pentecost.md lines 47 and 95 (the Introit's 'Ps. ibid., 1' and the Alleluia's 'Ps. 101, 2' inside the Latin blocks)
findings.problem: The typical edition prints the psalm-verse cue upright inside the italic antiphon to mark it as the Missal's editorial pointer and not as sung text, and the source says so explicitly with \textnormal{Ps.\ ibid., 1} inside the italic latinproper quote. The conversion preserves the distinction only as <span class="nodecor">, and release/public-alpha/assets/site.css defines .smallcaps but no rule for .nodecor, so the span is inert: the cue inherits the surrounding <em> and reads as part of the chant. The class is used the same inert way in the tracked editions of earlier propers, so this is a standing site-stylesheet gap rather than a fault introduced by this conversion, and the words themselves are correct and in place; what is lost is a distinction the Missal, the study and the converter all deliberately carry up to the last step.
findings.required_result: A .nodecor rule that restores upright setting (font-style: normal) is added to the site stylesheet, or the converter emits a form the site already styles, so that the psalm-verse cues inside the Latin antiphons read as cues and not as sung text.

observations.location: build/web/claude/liturgy/roman-rite/1962/propers/temporal/57-seventeenth-after-pentecost.md lines 498-500 ('## References' and the span that follows it)
observations.note: sections/90-apparatus.tex puts \label{sec:references} after the starred References heading rather than on it, so the anchor converts to a standalone in its own paragraph while the heading itself takes the auto-slug id 'references'. Every other section label became the heading's own {#sec:...} attribute. Nothing in the document links to either id, so nothing is broken today; recording it because a \label placed after a heading silently stops being that heading's anchor, and the next component that links to one would find out the hard way.

This is the canonical expansive study and not a concise or homily excerpt; no synthesis or homily prose appears in it. Limits: this is a Markdown, source, PDF-text and rendered-HTML review, not a browser review -- no headless browser, viewport, screenshot or CSS-cascade inspection was performed, and no external URL was fetched, so link liveness and visual presentation at any viewport are not certified here; the CSS judgement in WEB-003 rests on reading release/public-alpha/assets/site.css, not on a rendered page.
